title: Coval vs Cekura in 2026: Which Testing Platform Fits Regulated Teams?
summary: Coval vs Cekura compared on focus, human review, how real the simulated callers sound, seats, and pricing, and why regulated teams choose Coval.
body_markdown:
If your voice agent freezes cards, books patient appointments, or handles insurance claims, the platform that tests it has to do more than run simulated calls. Your QA and compliance teams need to trust its scores, and your security review will want a vendor with a track record in your industry. Judged that way, Coval vs Cekura comes down to focus, and Coval is the better fit. It’s built for enterprises in regulated industries, and its scores are checked by human reviewers on the calls your rules flag.


Coval is also the more established company. We’ve raised a[$28 million Series A](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-series-a/) , and our[founder](https://www.coval.ai/about-us/) , Brooke Hopkins, led evaluation infrastructure at Waymo before starting Coval. Cekura has raised a[$2.4 million](https://www.latestly.com/agency-news/latest-news-yc-backed-cekura-plans-to-open-office-in-india-following-usd-2-4-mn-fundraise-6971434.html) seed round.


On features, the two are close. Both test voice and chat agents, score your real production calls, turn failed calls into regression tests, and are SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant. They differ on who each platform is built for, whether you can trust its scores, how real its test calls sound, and what it costs to bring your whole team in.


Cekura’s entries come from its[pricing page](https://www.cekura.ai/pricing) and our September 2026 competitive review. Each row is explained in the sections below, with seats and pricing sharing the last one.

## Focus and track record: Coval is built for teams that can’t afford a failed call


In[financial services](https://www.coval.ai/industries/financial-services/) ,[healthcare](https://www.coval.ai/industries/healthcare/) , and[insurance](https://www.coval.ai/industries/insurance/) , a voice agent that gives one caller the wrong answer can become a compliance problem, not just a bad review. Those are the industries Coval is built for. Our approach comes from[self-driving cars](https://www.coval.ai/blog/coval-raises-3-3-to-to-bring-self-driving-car-simulation-to-ai-voice-chat-agents/) : a car proves itself in simulation before it drives a real street, and an agent should run through thousands of scenarios before a single customer hears it.


Chime shows what that looks like in a regulated business. Before each simulated call, Chime creates a test user with an API call. After the call, a follow-up API call checks the card status, account freezes, and other state changes the agent was supposed to produce. That way the test confirms the agent did the work, not just that it sounded like it did.


Chime and Perplexity are among the[more than 60 organizations](https://www.coval.ai/blog/new-self-improving-agents/) , including Fortune 500 enterprises, that trust Coval. Zoom’s QA team runs scheduled regression tests in Coval every day, and one click turns any live call into a new test. Our platform runs[3.1 million evaluation metrics](https://www.coval.ai/) every week. Cekura, by contrast, sells pay as you go or on a plan it names[Startup](https://www.cekura.ai/pricing) .


## Human review: Coval grades its AI judge against your QA team


A regulated team has to defend every score it reports, whether to an auditor, a compliance lead, or the engineer whose release a failed test just blocked. Scores for behavior, like whether the agent disclosed that it’s an AI, come from an[AI judge](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/types/llm-judge) : a language model that reads each call and answers a question you write. Each of those questions is a metric. We don’t ask you to take the judge’s word for it. Your own reviewers check it first.


That work happens in a[review project](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/human-review) , which groups the conversations to review, the metrics to label, and the people assigned to the work. Annotators, the reviewers who label calls, work in their own labeling view. Managers get a separate view to configure the project, manage reviewers, and track progress on a dashboard, so a whole QA or compliance team can label at scale. Auto-add rules keep the queue full: set a condition, such as every call where the disclosure metric failed, and matching conversations join the project as they come in. Annotators can also label blind, with the judge’s score hidden so it can’t sway them.


Reviewers don’t need to write code. The[review interface](https://www.coval.ai/products/human-review/) is built for QA analysts and compliance reviewers, who confirm, override, or annotate the judge’s verdicts inline. Every override, annotation, and verdict is tracked, so compliance has the audit trail it needs.


Agreement with your reviewers is the obvious test, and on its own it can mislead you. Say your reviewers mark 95 of 100 calls as successful and 5 as failures. A judge that passes all 100 agrees with them 95% of the time and catches none of the five failures.


Agreement can look healthy while the catch rate is zero. Example from Coval's human review docs.


So for each binary metric, meaning one with a yes-or-no answer, Coval’s[review insights](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/insights) put three numbers side by side: agreement, catch rate, and κ. Catch rate is the share of the failures your reviewers found that the judge also caught. κ (kappa) measures agreement beyond what chance alone would produce. The judge in that example scores 95% agreement and a catch rate of zero, and the second number is the one your compliance team cares about.


Your reviewers also catch the opposite problem: a judge that fails calls it should pass. In one[published case](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-to-create-ai-judge-metrics-you-can-trust/) , a team checking whether its outbound agent disclosed that it was an AI saw 89% agreement across 314 reviewed conversations, with 35 disagreements. Reading those 35 showed the metric was wrong, not the agent: in every disputed call, a wrong party had picked up or the caller had hung up early, so the agent never reached the point of disclosing anything. One paragraph added to the judge’s prompt fixed it, and rerunning the new judge on the same labeled calls turned those failures into passes that matched the reviewers.


Cekura routes flagged calls to an expert reviewer who can override the score. Coval builds review around your own QA and compliance team and turns their labels into numbers: agreement, catch rate, and κ tell you how much to trust each metric. If you don’t have a QA team to do the labeling, Coval’s own review team can label your calls and calibrate your metrics for you.


## Simulation: Coval’s test calls sound like your real ones, at production scale


A judge your reviewers trust can still only grade the calls it’s given. If your test calls are cleaner than the real ones, the judge will pass an agent that struggles with accents or a noisy line.


Each Coval test call is built around a[persona](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/personas/overview) , which sets the simulated caller’s voice, accent, personality, and speaking style. Add background sound from the built-in library or upload your own, and Coval mixes it into the caller’s side of the conversation for the length of the call. Your agent has to pick the caller’s words out of the noise, just as it will in production.


By default, the AI judge that grades those calls runs on the Coval Judge, a model we fine-tuned and paired with a custom judging algorithm. When you need to know how the agent holds up on its busiest day, Coval’s[load tests](https://docs.coval.ai/changelog) run up to 1,000 concurrent calls.


## Coval vs Cekura pricing: every seat included in the plan


Human review only works if your reviewers are in the tool, so the seat count matters as much as the test minutes. Every Coval plan comes with unlimited seats. Engineering, QA, and compliance each get their own workspace and permissions, with no charge for added seats.


As of November 2026, Coval’s[plans](https://www.coval.ai/pricing/) are Starter at $100 a month, Growth at $500 a month, and Enterprise from $4,500 a month. Every plan includes simulation, monitoring, and human review. Growth, the plan for teams with agents in production, covers 1,000 simulation minutes and 30,000 upload minutes (minutes of production calls you send to Coval for scoring) a month, along with unlimited metrics per call. Starter and Growth both begin with a 7-day free trial.


Cekura’s pricing page lists three plans. Pay as you go starts at $0 and charges $0.25 per minute of voice testing and $0.05 per monitored call, with one free seat and $30 a month for each seat after that. Startup costs $500 a month and includes 10 seats, and Enterprise is a custom annual contract.


Set the two $500 plans side by side and the difference is who gets in: Coval’s Growth plan covers your whole QA and compliance team, and Cekura’s Startup plan covers 10 people. On Coval, adding an eleventh reviewer, or a fiftieth, doesn’t change the price.


You can be running tests the same afternoon. The[Coval CLI](https://docs.coval.ai/welcome) gets you from install to a first simulation in under 15 minutes. If you’d rather have our team do the first pass, send us your agent’s phone number for a[free audit](https://www.coval.ai/voice-agent-audit/) : we’ll run 30+ simulations against each behavior you pick and send the results within two business days. Enterprise teams also get white-glove onboarding with a named engineer.

The clearest way to see the difference is on the call your compliance team worries about most. Start a 7-day trial, run that call against a persona with real background noise, and open a review project so a couple of your reviewers can label the results. By the end of the week, you’ll know your judge’s catch rate on the call that matters, and you’ll have the numbers to show compliance why you trust it.
